mainTopic: Rental disputes over boats and donkeys: unfinished trips, added cargo, what may be loaded, and who may ride
overview: The amud opens by finishing the discussion of רבי נתן's ruling about a rented boat that could not finish its trip. רב פפא explains that the money stays where it is only when both a specific boat and specific wine were agreed on; if neither was specified, the two sides split the fee. Next comes a ברייתא about a renter who 'unloads' the boat halfway: he pays for half the trip, and the owner has only a תרעומת (grievance). After a back-and-forth, the גמרא rereads the case: the renter loaded extra cargo midway. The owner's grievance is about the change from the deal or the extra rope. A second ברייתא sets what the renter and the donkey driver may load on a rented donkey. רב פפא explains the difference by their usual habits: drivers buy food at each stop, renters do not. A third ברייתא teaches which riders are allowed on a donkey rented for a man or for a woman, and רב פפא explains its mention of a pregnant woman as one who is also nursing. אביי learns from this that a fish's weight goes by its belly, which matters when buying and selling.

steps.title: The owner could ask for the wine and bring a new boat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the case behind רבי נתן's ruling. The boat owner could say, 'Give me that wine, and I will bring another boat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the owner say to him: Give me that wine, and I will bring a boat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues its question about which case רבי נתן's ruling is talking about. It points out that the boat owner has an argument: he can bring another boat, so let the renter bring the wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The specific wine is now lost, so the renter cannot hand it over. That makes the renter the one who cannot keep the deal, and it seems he should have to pay. This pushes against the ruling that the money simply stays wherever it is.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him say to him (one side could argue this)

phrases.english: Let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The first 'him' is the boat owner, and he is talking to the renter.

phrases.english: Give me that wine
and I will bring a boat.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא לֵיהּ: הַב לִי הָהוּא חַמְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier part of the daf, which was trying to define the case of רבי נתן's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of רבי נתן's ruling about a boat that sank halfway
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner can offer another boat, but the renter can no longer produce that wine. So the renter seems to be the one breaking the deal and should have to pay.

steps.title: רב פפא: the ruling applies only to this boat and this wine
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא limits רבי נתן's ruling to a case where both the boat and the wine were specified. If neither was specified, the two sides split the fee.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: You only find this ruling in a case of 'this boat and this wine.' But with an unspecified boat and unspecified wine, they split.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by narrowing the case. רבי נתן was only talking about a deal for a specific boat and specific wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When both the boat and the wine were specified and both are gone, neither side can keep the deal. So neither side can make demands of the other, and the money stays where it is. When neither was specified, both sides could still carry out the deal, so they divide the fee: the renter pays half.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer
You only find this case in...
This specific boat and this specific wine

steps.whatToRemember: רבי נתן's ruling, where the money stays where it is, applies when both the boat and the wine were specified. If neither was specified, the two sides split the fee.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
You do not find it
phrases.notes: 'It' means the case of רבי נתן's ruling.

phrases.english: except with this boat and this wine.
But with an unspecified boat and unspecified wine,
they split.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ אֶלָּא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought the owner could always demand the wine and offer another boat.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is one where both the boat and the wine were specified, so neither side can make demands. When neither was specified, they split the fee.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the renter unloads the boat halfway
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if someone rents a boat and unloads it halfway, he pays for half the trip. The owner has only a grievance against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If someone rents a boat and unloads it halfway through the trip, he pays the owner for half the trip. The owner has nothing against him except a grievance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a renter who stops halfway and unloads his cargo. This opens a new topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling has two parts. The renter only has to pay for the half he used. The owner cannot collect more money, but he does have a moral complaint against the renter.

keyTerms.meaning: A grievance, a complaint with no money claim

steps.confusionAlert: תרעומת does not mean the owner can collect anything. It only means the renter treated him unfairly.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who rents the boat
and unloaded it halfway through the journey,

phrases.aramaic: נוֹתֵן לוֹ שְׂכָרוֹ שֶׁל חֲצִי הַדֶּרֶךְ,
phrases.english: gives him his fee for half the journey,
and he has nothing against him but a grievance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, related case about rented boats.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A renter who unloads halfway pays for half the trip. The owner has only a grievance.

steps.title: Which case is this? Either way it seems wrong
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what situation the ברייתא means. Both possible readings seem to fail.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the owner can find someone else to rent the boat, why does he have a grievance? And if he cannot find anyone, the renter should have to pay the full fee!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to picture the ברייתא's case. It shows that each option clashes with the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner can re-rent the boat, he loses nothing, so there seems to be no reason for a grievance. If he cannot re-rent it, the renter broke the deal and caused a loss, so he should pay the full amount. Either way, 'half the fee plus a grievance' seems not to fit.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If we say that he can find someone to rent it to,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the boat owner, finding a new renter for the second half of the trip.

phrases.english: why does he have a grievance?
And if he cannot find someone to rent it to,
he should have to pay its entire fee!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִילֵּימָא דְּקָא מַשְׁכַּח לְאֹגוֹרַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the case of the ברייתא brought in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling of half the fee plus only a grievance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is a two-sided trap. If the owner can re-rent the boat, he has no reason for a grievance. If he cannot, the renter should owe the full fee.

steps.title: The owner can re-rent; the grievance is for wear on the boat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the owner can find another renter. His grievance comes from the extra wear on the boat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the owner can find someone to rent it to. So why does he have a grievance? Because of the wear and tear on the boat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks the first option: the owner can re-rent the boat. It then explains what the grievance is about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unloading halfway and loading a new renter's cargo puts extra strain on the boat. That is the reason the owner feels wronged, even though he loses no rental income.

phrases.english: Actually, it is where he can find someone to rent it to,
but why does he have a grievance?
Because of the wear and tear on the boat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two-sided challenge in step 4 by choosing the first option.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case and explaining the reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the owner can re-rent the boat, there seems to be no reason for any grievance.
steps.terutzMaskana: He can re-rent it, but the boat suffers extra wear, and that is the grievance.

steps.title: If the boat was worn down, that is a real money claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer. Damage to the boat should give the owner an actual claim for money, not just a grievance.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, that is a proper claim, and he should have money owed to him by the renter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave. Real physical wear on the boat sounds like something the renter should pay for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A grievance is supposed to be a complaint with no money attached. But extra wear on the boat is a real, measurable loss, so the owner should be able to collect for it. This means the explanation in step 5 does not fit the ברייתא's wording of 'only a grievance.'

phrases.english: If so,
it is a proper claim
and he has money owed to him by the other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the grievance is about wear on the boat
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Physical damage is a real loss, which should give a money claim. That clashes with the ברייתא saying the owner has only a grievance.

steps.title: A new reading: the renter loaded more cargo midway
steps.stepSummary: After the challenge in Step 6, the גמרא rereads פרקה. It means the renter loaded more of his own cargo into the boat halfway through, so he pays for that extra load only for the second half.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what does 'unloaded it' mean? That he unloaded his cargo into it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the earlier reading of the ברייתא and gives the word פרקה a new meaning: the renter added more cargo into the boat halfway through the trip.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the old reading, the renter emptied the boat midway, and wear on the boat would have meant a real money claim. Under the new reading, he added extra cargo for the second half, so 'paying half' means paying for the added load only for the half of the trip it was carried.

keyTerms.meaning: He unloaded it; here reread as unloading his goods into the boat

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'unloading' does not mean taking cargo off the boat. It means unloading more goods from somewhere else onto the boat.

phrases.english: Rather, what does 'unloaded it' mean?
That he unloaded his cargo into it.
phrases.notes: He means the renter added more of his own goods into the boat halfway through the trip.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 6 by giving the case in the ברייתא a new meaning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the ברייתא (case redefinition)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: פרקה meant the renter emptied the boat midway, which would cause wear and a real damages claim.
steps.terutzMaskana: פרקה means the renter loaded extra cargo midway, so he pays for it only for the second half of the trip.

steps.title: If so, why does the owner have any grievance?
steps.stepSummary: With the new reading, the גמרא asks what the owner's תרעומת could be, since the renter is paying for the extra cargo.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, what is the grievance?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question on its own new reading: if the renter pays for the extra load, what is the owner upset about? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the owner has only a תרעומת. Under the new reading the owner seems fully paid, so it is unclear why he should have any complaint at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A grievance, a moral complaint that cannot be collected in court

phrases.english: But then, what is the grievance?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the new reading of Step 7 against the ברייתא's word 'grievance'.
steps.kashyaTarget: The new reading of פרקה from Step 7
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the renter pays for the extra cargo, the owner loses nothing, so the ברייתא should not mention any תרעומת.

steps.title: The grievance: a change from the deal, or extra rope
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives two explanations of the owner's תרעומת: the renter changed the original plan, or the owner needed extra rope to tie down the added cargo.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of the change of mind. Alternatively, because of the extra rope.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the owner is upset because the renter did something different from what they agreed, or because the extra load needed more rope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither reason is a real money loss that a court would order paid, so it fits the ברייתא's word תרעומת. The change from the deal is a matter of feelings, and the extra rope is a small bother.

keyTerms.meaning: A change of mind, going against the original plan

steps.whatToRemember: The boat ברייתא is now read this way: the renter added cargo midway and pays for it only for the second half. The owner's only complaint is the change from the deal or the extra rope.

phrases.english: Because of the change of mind.
Alternatively, because of the extra rope.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: With the extra cargo paid for, the owner has no reason to complain.
steps.terutzMaskana: He complains because the deal was changed, or because he needed extra rope. Neither gives him a money claim.

steps.title: What a renter and a donkey driver may load on a rented donkey
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: someone who rents a donkey to ride may load his garment, water jug, and food for the whole trip. The donkey driver may load barley, hay, and his own food for one day only. Beyond that, each one can stop the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: One who rents a donkey to ride on it: the renter may place on it his garment, his water jug, and food for that journey. Beyond this, the donkey driver may stop him. The donkey driver may place on it barley, hay, and his own food for that day. Beyond this, the renter may stop him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the limits of what each side may put on a rented donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renter gets food for the whole journey, but the חמר gets food for only one day. That difference is what the גמרא questions next.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages taught; introduces a ברייתא

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One who rents a donkey to ride on it:
the renter may place on it his garment and his water jug
and food for that journey;
beyond this, the donkey driver may stop him.
The donkey driver may place on it barley and hay
and his own food for that day;
beyond this, the renter may stop him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַשּׂוֹכֵר אֶת הַחֲמוֹר לִרְכּוֹב עָלֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: renting a donkey instead of a boat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The renter may load food for the whole trip. The donkey driver may load his own food for only one day. Each can stop the other from loading more.

steps.title: Why should the renter and the driver be treated differently?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the case. If food can be bought on the road, the driver should be able to stop the renter from bringing food for the whole trip. If food cannot be bought, the renter should not be able to stop the driver from bringing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are the circumstances? If food is available to buy, the donkey driver should also be able to stop him. And if food is not available to buy, the renter should also not be able to stop him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: whichever way you picture the road, the renter and the driver should get the same rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether food is easy to buy on the way does not depend on who is buying. So the different rules for the שוכר and the חמר seem to make no sense either way.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If food is available to buy,
the donkey driver should also be able to stop him;
phrases.notes: He means the driver should be able to stop the renter from bringing food for the whole trip.

phrases.english: and if food is not available to buy,
the renter should also not be able to stop him!

steps.kashyaTarget: The different rules for the renter and the donkey driver in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whether food can be bought on the road is the same for both of them, so either both may bring food for the whole trip or neither may.

steps.title: רב פפא: drivers usually buy food at each stop, renters do not
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the ברייתא speaks of a road where food can be bought at each stop, but only with some effort. Donkey drivers usually make that effort, and renters usually do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It is needed only where food can be bought if one takes the trouble to buy it from station to station. A donkey driver's way is to take the trouble and buy. A renter's way is not to take the trouble and buy.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge. He says the difference between the two people comes from their usual habits on the road, not from whether food is available.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food is available, but buying it takes effort at each stop. A חמר travels the road for a living and normally buys as he goes, so he may load food for one day only. A שוכר does not usually do this, so he may bring food for the whole trip.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for a certain case
A station, an inn along the road

steps.whatToRemember: In renting, each side's rights follow normal practice. The driver is expected to buy food at each stop, but the renter may bring food for the whole trip.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that what each side may expect in a rental depends on how people in each role normally behave, not just on what is possible.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: It is needed only
where food can be bought if one takes the trouble to buy it
from station to station.
phrases.notes: These are rest stops along the road where travelers could buy supplies.

phrases.english: A donkey driver's way is to take the trouble and buy.
A renter's way is not to take the trouble and buy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 11 by defining the exact case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (לא צריכא), based on the usual habits of each side
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Food is either available or not, so the renter and the driver should be treated the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: Food is available with effort. The driver normally makes that effort, but the renter does not, so their rights differ.

steps.title: Who may ride a donkey rented for a man or for a woman
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: a donkey rented for a man may not carry a woman. A donkey rented for a woman may carry a man, or any woman: adult or young, even pregnant, even nursing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: If someone rents a donkey for a man to ride, a woman may not ride it. If he rents it for a woman, a man may ride it. And if it was rented for a woman, any woman may ride it, adult or young, even a pregnant woman, and even a nursing woman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about who is allowed to ride a donkey, depending on who it was rented for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule only works in one direction: 'rented for a man' does not allow a woman, but 'rented for a woman' does allow a man. So the ברייתא treats a woman rider as harder on the donkey than a man. Once a donkey is rented for a woman, the owner cannot object to any woman, even one who adds extra weight.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages taught. This opens a ברייתא.
A nursing woman, who brings her baby along

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the man is the 'heavier' case that gets restricted. The ברייתא says the opposite: rented for a man means no woman, while rented for a woman means a man is allowed.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One who rents a donkey
for a man to ride on it,
a woman may not ride on it.
If it was rented for a woman, a man may ride on it.
And if rented for a woman, any woman may ride, adult or young,
even a pregnant woman,
and even a nursing woman.
phrases.notes: A nursing mother takes her baby with her, so the donkey carries two people.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַשּׂוֹכֵר אֶת הַחֲמוֹר לִרְכּוֹב עָלֶיהָ אִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of renting a donkey to ride (step 10). It moves from how much baggage may be loaded to which riders are allowed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rented for a man means no woman may ride. Rented for a woman means a man may ride, and so may any woman, even pregnant or nursing.

steps.title: Why list pregnant after nursing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if even a nursing woman, who brings a whole baby along, is allowed, why does the ברייתא need to say a pregnant woman is allowed?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you said even a nursing woman may ride, do you really need to say a pregnant woman may?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the order of the ברייתא's list, since the 'even' cases seem to go in the wrong order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא that says 'even X, and even Y' usually goes from the smaller חידוש to the bigger one. A nursing woman with her baby is clearly more weight than a pregnant woman. So once nursing is allowed, pregnant seems obvious and extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it needed? Isn't it obvious?

phrases.english: Now that you said a nursing woman may ride,
is it needed to say a pregnant woman may?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the wording of the ברייתא from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'אפילו מעוברת ואפילו מניקה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the heavier case (nursing) is allowed, the lighter case (pregnant) is obvious, so mentioning it is extra.

steps.title: רב פפא: a woman who is both pregnant and nursing
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the ברייתא means a pregnant woman who is also nursing. That is even more weight than nursing alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The ברייתא means a woman who is pregnant and also nursing.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by rereading the case: the pregnant woman is also nursing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the list builds up properly. Even a nursing woman may ride, and even one who is nursing and pregnant at the same time, which is the heaviest case. So 'pregnant' is not extra. It adds weight on top of nursing.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who answers the question

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It is speaking of a pregnant woman who is also nursing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: מְעוּבֶּרֶת וְהִיא מְנִיקָה קָאָמַר
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: two separate cases become one combined case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pregnant and nursing were two separate cases, so 'pregnant' looked obvious and extra.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Pregnant' means pregnant and also nursing, the heaviest case, so it adds something new.

steps.title: אביי: a fish's weight follows its belly
steps.stepSummary: אביי learns from the ברייתא that a fish's weight depends on the size of its belly.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Learn from this that the weight of a fish is in its belly.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי draws a side lesson from the ברייתא's idea that pregnancy adds real weight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא counts a pregnant woman as heavier because of her belly. אביי applies the same idea to fish: a fish with a bigger belly weighs more. This is a practical lesson learned from the case, not a new rule about donkeys.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Learn from this
that a fish's weight goes by its belly.
phrases.notes: He means a fish with a bigger belly weighs more, just as a pregnant woman counts as heavier.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ בִּינִיתָא אַכְּרֵסַהּ תָּקְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a side lesson on the idea, from steps 13 and 15, that pregnancy adds weight.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Weight increases with the size of the belly, so a fish's weight is judged by its belly.

steps.title: What practical difference does אביי's lesson make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical use there is in knowing that a fish's weight follows its belly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question to set up the next line, which gives the practical use of אביי's lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on אביי. The גמרא simply wants to know where his observation about fish matters in real life.

keyTerms.meaning: Practical difference (literally: what comes out of it)

phrases.english: What practical difference does this make?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical use of אביי's statement in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what real-life situation does it matter that a fish's weight follows its belly?

steps.title: It matters for buying and selling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the lesson matters for buying and selling fish, so people can judge a fish's weight and price fairly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: אביי's lesson helps in business dealings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When fish are sold by weight, knowing that a big belly means more weight helps the buyer and seller set a fair price.
steps.whatToRemember: Rented for a man means no woman; rented for a woman means any rider is allowed, even a woman who is pregnant and nursing (רב פפא). From this אביי learns that weight follows the belly, which matters when selling fish.

phrases.english: For buying and selling.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The lesson helps people judge a fish's weight, and so its price, when buying and selling.
